title: Data Science and Data Visualisation
summary: Turn raw data into answers: ask good questions, collect and clean data, find patterns with averages and correlation, choose honest charts and tell a clear story with data.
learn: The stages of the data science cycle
How to collect data fairly, including from open data
How to use averages, range and correlation to find patterns
How to choose the right chart and spot misleading ones
How to tell a story with data while protecting privacy
intro: Data scientists help hospitals plan beds, sports teams pick players and councils plan bus routes. In this topic you follow the same process: ask a question, collect data, clean up its mistakes, find the patterns, make charts that tell the truth, and present your findings without breaking anyone's privacy.

pages.title: What is data science?
pages.spec: Describe what data science is and the stages of the data science cycle
pages.summary: Data science is using data to answer questions and make decisions. Data scientists follow a cycle: ask a question, collect data, clean it, analyse it, visualise it and communicate the findings.
pages.starter: Your phone knows how many steps you walked every day this year. What questions could you answer with that data?

I can name the six stages of the data science cycle

b: Data science means using data to answer questions and make better decisions
Which bus routes need more buses at 8am?
Which players should a football club sign?
When will A&E be busiest this winter?
1 Ask a clear question
2 Collect the data
3 Clean it
4 Analyse it to find patterns
5 Visualise it with charts
6 Communicate the answer, then ask the next question
Some datasets are enormous: billions of rows, arriving every second
Volume (how much), velocity (how fast), variety (how many kinds)
Examples: card payments, weather sensors, streaming services, smart meters

blocks.text: What is data science?

**[[data]]** is raw facts and figures, such as numbers, words, dates or measurements. On its own it doesn't mean much. **[[data science]]** is the use of data to answer questions, spot patterns and make better decisions. Data scientists combine maths, computing and knowledge of the subject they're studying.

Question
Data used
rows: Which player creates the most chances?
Passes, positions and shots in every match

blocks.text: The data science cycle

items: **Ask** a clear question that data can answer.
**Collect** the data you need.
**Clean** it: fix or remove mistakes and gaps.
**Analyse** it to find patterns, using averages, comparisons and correlation.
**Visualise** it using charts and graphs.
**Communicate** what you found, then ask the next question.

blocks.text: Big data

**[[big data]]** means datasets so large or fast-moving that ordinary tools can't handle them. Big data is often described by the "3 Vs": **volume** (huge amounts), **velocity** (arriving quickly, often in real time) and **variety** (many types, such as numbers, text, images and sensor readings).
A good data question is specific and measurable. "Are pupils tired?" is vague. "Do pupils who sleep less than 8 hours score lower on Monday quizzes?" is something data can answer.

blocks.title: Sharpen the question
steps: Read the five vague questions on the board (e.g. "Is the canteen good?").
Rewrite each as a specific, measurable question that data could answer.
For one of them, list what data you would need to collect.

q.q: Write your improved version of "Is the canteen good?" and the data you'd need.
q.a: E.g. "Which canteen meals sell out fastest, and which have the most food wasted?" Data: sales per meal per day, time each meal sells out, weight of food waste per meal.

q.q: Why is a specific question better for data science?
q.a: It tells you exactly what data to collect and how to measure the answer, so you can actually reach a clear conclusion.

o: Using data to answer questions and make decisions

check.why: Big data is huge, fast, varied data.

practice.a: Ask, collect, clean, analyse, visualise, communicate (3 marks all correct; 2 for four or five in order; 1 for two or three).

practice.q: Give one example of how data science could help a hospital.
practice.a: A suitable question (1) and the data used (1), e.g. predicting busy times in A&E using past visit numbers and weather.

pages.title: Collecting data
pages.spec: Collect data fairly and describe different types and sources of data
pages.summary: Data can be qualitative or quantitative, and collected first-hand (primary) or from others (secondary), including free open data. How you collect it, and from whom, decides whether your answer is fair.
pages.starter: You want to know the most popular sport in school, but you only ask the rugby team. What's wrong with your data?
sc: I can tell the difference between qualitative and quantitative data
I can compare primary and secondary data and use open data
I can explain how sampling can make data biased

b: Quantitative: numbers you can measure or count (height, score, minutes)
Qualitative: descriptions, categories or opinions ("great", "blue", "rugby")
Many datasets have both
The type decides which charts and calculations you can use
Primary data: you collect it yourself (survey, experiment, sensor)
Secondary data: someone else collected it (websites, government statistics)
Open data: free for anyone to use, e.g. OpenDataNI, data.gov.uk
Always check who collected secondary data, when and how
slides.n: OpenDataNI (opendatani.gov.uk) has datasets on Northern Ireland such as bike-share use, air quality and public toilets. Great for real projects.

b: A sample is the group you collect data from
Biased sample: only asking the rugby team about favourite sports
Fair samples are big enough and represent everyone
Survey questions must be clear and not lead people to an answer

blocks.text: Types of data

blocks.caption: Quantitative or qualitative?
head: Type
What it is
Examples
rows: Numbers you can measure or count
Height in cm, test score, minutes of screen time

blocks.text: Primary, secondary and open data

**[[primary data]]** is data you collect yourself, for example with a survey, an experiment or a sensor. It fits your question exactly, but takes time. **[[secondary data]]** has already been collected by someone else, such as government statistics or a sports website. It's quick to get, but you need to check who collected it, when, and how.

**[[open data]]** is data that anyone is allowed to use for free. Governments and organisations publish open data on things like air quality, weather, transport and population. In Northern Ireland, the OpenDataNI portal has hundreds of datasets.
Sampling and bias

Usually you can't ask everyone, so you collect data from a **[[sample]]**. If your sample isn't representative, your results will be biased. Asking only the rugby team about the school's favourite sport will obviously over-count rugby!

blocks.title: Fair data collection
items: Choose a sample that represents everyone you want to know about
Make the sample large enough
Write clear, neutral questions ("Which sport do you enjoy most?", not "Don't you agree football is the best?")
Give answer options that cover everyone, including "Other" or "None"
Ask permission and don't collect more personal data than you need

blocks.title: Survey design
steps: Choose a question about school life (e.g. "How do pupils travel to school, and how long does it take?").
Write a 5-question survey with at least one quantitative and one qualitative question.
Swap with another group. Find any leading, unclear or missing options in their survey.
Plan your sample: who will you ask, and how many?

q.q: Write your two best survey questions and say whether each collects quantitative or qualitative data.
q.a: E.g. "How many minutes does your journey to school usually take?" (quantitative); "How do you usually travel to school? Walk / Bus / Car / Bike / Other" (qualitative).

q.q: Describe your sample and explain why it is fair.
q.a: E.g. "20 pupils from every year group, chosen from different form classes, so every age is represented."

o: The first row of a table
Data anyone is allowed to use for free

practice.a: Primary: collected yourself, e.g. your own survey (1); secondary: collected by someone else, e.g. government statistics (1).

practice.q: Rewrite this leading question to be fair: "Don't you agree school should start later?"

pages.title: Cleaning data
pages.spec: Identify and fix common problems in messy data
pages.summary: Real data is messy: typos, inconsistent formats, duplicates, missing values and impossible outliers. Cleaning it before analysis is essential, and data scientists often spend more time cleaning than analysing.
pages.starter: In a survey, people typed their year group as "8", "Y8", "year 8", "eight" and "8A". How many different year groups would a computer think there are?
sc: I can identify common problems in messy data
I can fix inconsistent, duplicate and missing data
I can decide what to do with outliers

b: Inconsistent formats: "8", "Y8", "Year 8"
Typos: "Enniskilen", "Eniskillen"
Duplicates: the same response entered twice
Missing values: blank cells
Impossible values: age 250, height 1.6 cm
Choose one standard format and convert everything to it
Remove exact duplicates
Decide how to handle blanks: remove the row, or leave it out of that calculation
Check outliers: mistake or real?
Keep a record of every change you make
Analysis of dirty data gives wrong answers
Data scientists often say most of their time goes on cleaning
Spreadsheets help: sort, filter, find and replace, remove duplicates
Validation when collecting data stops many problems happening

blocks.text: Why clean data?

Real-world data is almost never perfect. People make typos, write things in different ways, skip questions or submit a form twice. If you analyse dirty data, your answers will be wrong, so **[[data cleaning]]** (finding and fixing problems) comes before analysis. Professional data scientists often say this takes up most of their time.

blocks.caption: Common data problems and fixes
head: Problem
Example
Fix
rows: Convert all to one format, e.g. 8
Remove the row or leave it out of that calculation, and say so
Check: probably a typo for 25; if unsure, remove it

blocks.text: Outliers

An **[[outlier]]** is a value very different from the rest. Some outliers are **mistakes** (someone typed 600 minutes of homework instead of 60). Others are **real** and interesting (one pupil really does run 15 km a week). Never just delete outliers because they're inconvenient: check whether they're possible and explain what you did.
Prevent problems by using validation when you collect data: drop-down lists instead of typing, number-only fields, and range checks (e.g. age 11 to 19).

blocks.title: Clean the canteen survey
steps: Open the messy "Canteen survey" spreadsheet your teacher gives you (30 responses).
Find and fix: inconsistent year groups, typos in meal names, duplicates and blanks.
Find two outliers. Decide for each: mistake or real? Fix or keep?
Write a "cleaning log" listing every change you made.

q.q: Write three entries from your cleaning log.
q.a: E.g. "Changed 'Y8', 'year 8' and 'eight' to 8 (6 cells). Removed duplicate response from row 17 (identical to row 16). Changed 'chiken curry' to 'Chicken curry' (2 cells)."

q.q: Describe one outlier and what you decided to do with it, with a reason.
q.a: E.g. "Someone said they spend £45 a day in the canteen. That's impossible for a school lunch, probably £4.50, but I can't be sure, so I removed it and noted it in the log."

o: Finding and fixing problems in data before analysis

check.q: Which is an example of inconsistent formatting?
o: A blank row at the end
A value very different from the rest

check.q: What should you do with an outlier?
o: Check whether it's a mistake or real before deciding

practice.q: Describe three problems that can make data "dirty".
practice.a: Any three: inconsistent formats (1); typos (1); duplicates (1); missing values (1); impossible values/errors (1).

practice.q: Explain how validation can reduce the need for data cleaning.
practice.a: Validation checks data as it's entered, e.g. drop-downs/range checks (1), so many errors are stopped before they get into the data (1).

pages.title: Finding patterns
pages.spec: Use averages, range and correlation to analyse data, and explain why correlation is not causation
pages.summary: Averages (mean, median, mode) summarise data, and range shows spread. Correlation shows whether two variables change together, but it doesn't prove that one causes the other.
pages.starter: Towns with more ice-cream sales also have more sunburn. Does ice cream cause sunburn?
sc: I can calculate the mean, median, mode and range
I can describe positive, negative and no correlation
I can explain why correlation doesn't prove causation

b: Mean: add them all up, divide by how many
Median: the middle value when in order
Mode: the most common value
Range: biggest minus smallest, which shows how spread out data is
Positive: as one goes up, the other goes up (revision time and test score)
Negative: as one goes up, the other goes down (screen time before bed and sleep)
None: no link (shoe size and test score)
Scatter graphs show correlation clearly
Ice-cream sales and sunburn rise together, but ice cream doesn't cause sunburn
A third factor (hot sunny weather) causes both
Sometimes it's pure coincidence
To show causation you need a fair experiment, not just a pattern

blocks.text: Averages and range

blocks.caption: Summary statistics
head: Measure
How to work it out
Best for
rows: Add all values, divide by how many there are
Put values in order and take the middle one
The value that appears most often
Showing how spread out data is

blocks.title: Minutes of homework
blocks.context: Seven pupils did this many minutes of homework: 20, 35, 40, 40, 45, 50, 180
steps: Median = the 4th value in order = 40 minutes
Mode = 40 minutes (appears twice); Range = 180 - 20 = 160 minutes
blocks.answer: The outlier (180) pulls the mean up to about 59, so the median (40) is a better "typical" value here.

blocks.text: Correlation

**[[correlation]]** describes whether two things change together. On a **scatter graph**, points that go upwards from left to right show **positive** correlation; points going downwards show **negative** correlation; points scattered randomly show **no** correlation.
Correlation is not causation

**[[causation]]** means one thing actually causes another. Just because two things are correlated doesn't mean one causes the other. Ice-cream sales and sunburn both rise in hot weather, so the **third factor** (sunshine) causes both. Other correlations are pure coincidence. To prove causation, scientists use fair experiments that change one thing and keep everything else the same.
News headlines often confuse correlation with causation, e.g. "People who eat breakfast earn more!" Ask: could something else explain this?

blocks.title: Analyse the class data
steps: Use the class dataset your teacher provides (e.g. hours of sleep, minutes of exercise and quiz scores, all anonymous).
Calculate the mean, median, mode and range of the quiz scores.
Draw a scatter graph of sleep against quiz score. Describe the correlation.
Suggest one other factor that might explain the pattern.

q.q: Write your mean, median, mode and range, and say which average best represents the data.
q.a: Answers depend on the data; a good answer shows working and chooses the median if there are outliers, explaining why.

q.q: Describe the correlation and give one reason it might not mean sleep causes better scores.
q.a: E.g. "Weak positive correlation: more sleep goes with slightly higher scores. But pupils who sleep more might also revise more or have fewer late activities, so something else could be the cause."

check.why: The middle value in order is 8.

check.q: Revision time and test scores both go up together. This is...

o: A third factor or coincidence might explain the link

practice.q: Calculate the mean, mode and range of: 5, 8, 8, 10, 14.
A study finds pupils with more books at home get better grades. Explain why this doesn't prove books cause better grades.
practice.a: Correlation doesn't show causation (1); another factor such as family income/support/reading habits could cause both (1).

pages.title: Charts that tell the truth
pages.spec: Choose suitable charts for different data and identify misleading visualisations
pages.summary: The right chart depends on the data and the question: bar charts compare categories, line graphs show change over time, scatter graphs show relationships and pie charts show parts of a whole. Charts can mislead through tricks such as cut-off axes and cherry-picked data.
pages.starter: Look at the two charts on the board showing the same sales figures. Why does one look like a disaster and the other look fine?
sc: I can choose the right chart for a dataset
I can spot four ways charts mislead
I can improve a misleading chart

b: Bar chart: compare categories (favourite sport)
Line graph: change over time (temperature each month)
Scatter graph: relationship between two numbers (height and arm span)
Pie chart: parts of a whole, only with a few categories
Cut-off axis: starting at 95 instead of 0 makes small differences look huge
Cherry-picking: only showing the months that suit your story
Wrong chart type: a pie chart that doesn't add up to 100%
Misleading pictures: 3D effects and icons that distort sizes
slides.n: Show the classic truncated-axis example: two bars of 96 and 98 that look like one is double the other.

b: Clear title saying what the chart shows
Labelled axes with units
Start bar chart axes at zero
Show where the data came from

blocks.text: Data visualisation

**[[data visualisation]]** means showing data as a picture, such as a chart, graph, map or infographic. A good visualisation makes patterns obvious at a glance. The most important skill is choosing the right type for your data and your question.

blocks.caption: Which chart?
head: Chart
Use it to
Example
rows: Number of pupils choosing each sport
Show the relationship between two numbers
Hours of sleep against quiz score
Show parts of a whole (few categories)

blocks.text: Misleading charts
A **[[misleading chart]]** gives the wrong impression even if the numbers are true.

blocks.title: Tricks to watch for
items: Truncated **[[axis]]**: the y-axis starts above zero, exaggerating differences
Cherry-picking: showing only the data that supports one story
Uneven scales: gaps on the axis that aren't equal
Pie charts that don't add up to 100%, or have too many slices
3D effects or picture icons that make some values look bigger than they are

blocks.title: The truncated axis
blocks.context: A bar chart shows Brand A at 96% and Brand B at 98% satisfaction. The y-axis starts at 95%.
steps: Brand B's bar looks three times as tall as Brand A's.
Redraw the chart with the y-axis starting at 0.
Now the bars are almost the same height, which is the honest picture.
blocks.answer: The difference is only 2 percentage points. Starting at 95% made it look huge.

blocks.title: Chart doctor
steps: Your teacher gives you four "sick" charts from fictional adverts and news stories.
Diagnose what's wrong with each one.
Redraw one chart honestly (by hand or in a spreadsheet) and compare the impression it gives.

q.q: For one chart, describe the trick and the impression it gives.
q.a: E.g. "The y-axis starts at 50 so a rise from 52 to 55 looks enormous. It makes the company look far more successful than it is."

q.q: Which chart type would you choose to show how a town's population changed from 1990 to 2025, and why?
q.a: A line graph, because it shows change over time clearly.

check.q: Which chart is best for showing change over time?
check.why: Line graphs show trends over time.

check.q: Which chart shows the relationship between two numerical variables?
Why can a y-axis starting at 90 instead of 0 mislead?
o: It makes small differences look much bigger
Only showing data that supports your point

practice.q: State the best chart type for each: (a) favourite fruit of 30 pupils; (b) daily temperature for a month.
practice.a: (a) bar chart (or pie chart) (1); (b) line graph (1).

practice.q: Describe three features of an honest, well-designed chart.
practice.a: Any three: clear title (1); labelled axes with units (1); axis starting at zero for bar charts (1); source shown (1); suitable chart type (1); no distorting 3D effects (1).

pages.title: Data stories and privacy
pages.spec: Present findings as a data story and protect people's privacy when using data
pages.summary: A data story combines a clear message, the right chart and context so people understand and act on the findings. Data about people must be handled legally and ethically, removing details that could identify anyone.
pages.starter: A headline says "Year 9 pupil spends 9 hours a day on their phone!" The school survey had only one Year 9 pupil from 9C. What's the problem?
sc: I can present findings as a clear data story
I can explain how to anonymise data
I can describe how UK GDPR protects personal data

b: Start with your question and your headline finding
Show the one chart that proves it best
Give context: how much data, from whom, any limits
Finish with what should happen next
A dashboard shows several key charts and numbers on one screen
Often updated live from new data
Used by hospitals, councils, shops and sports teams
Good dashboards show only what matters for decisions
Personal data: anything that identifies a living person
Anonymise: remove names and details that could identify someone
Small groups can still identify people ("the only Year 9 in 9C")
UK GDPR: collect only what you need, keep it secure, use it fairly

blocks.text: Telling a data story
Charts alone don't change anything. A **[[data story]]** explains what the data shows, why it matters and what should happen next. A good data story has:

items: A clear question and a one-sentence headline answer
The best chart to support it, clearly labelled
Context: how much data, collected from whom, and any limitations
A recommendation or next step

blocks.text: A **[[dashboard]]** shows several important charts and numbers on one screen, often updating automatically. Councils use dashboards to track bin collections, hospitals use them to see waiting times, and football clubs use them to monitor player fitness.
Privacy and personal data
**[[personal data]]** is any information that could identify a living person, such as a name, address, photo, email or school ID number. When you work with data about people you must protect it.

To **[[anonymise]]** data means removing or changing details so that no one can be identified. This isn't just deleting names: in a small group, details like "the only left-handed pupil in 9C" can still identify someone. Data scientists combine groups or remove rare details to prevent this.
The law: UK GDPR

**[[UK GDPR]]** and the Data Protection Act 2018 set rules for using personal data in the UK. Organisations must collect only the data they need, use it only for the reason they gave, keep it accurate and secure, and not keep it longer than necessary. People have the right to see the data held about them.
You studied data protection law in more detail in the "Digital Ethics, the Law and the Planet" topic.

blocks.title: Data story project
steps: Use your cleaned survey data (lesson 3) or an OpenDataNI dataset your teacher provides.
Write your question and a one-sentence headline answer.
Create the one chart that best supports it, with a title, labels and source.
Check privacy: could anyone be identified? Fix it if so.
Present your data story to the class in 90 seconds.

q.q: Write your question, headline answer and recommendation.
q.a: E.g. "Question: how do pupils travel to school? Headline: 41% come by car even though most live under 2 miles away. Recommendation: start a walking-bus scheme for pupils living nearby."

q.q: Explain one privacy risk in your data and how you dealt with it.
q.a: E.g. "Only one pupil cycled from Lisnaskea, so they could be identified. I combined small villages into 'Other areas' before making the chart."

o: A clear explanation of what data shows, why it matters and what to do next
A screen showing key charts and figures together
check.why: Dashboards summarise data at a glance.

check.q: What does it mean to anonymise data?
o: Remove details that could identify people
collect only the personal data they need
check.why: Data minimisation is a key principle.

practice.q: Explain why removing names is not always enough to anonymise data.
practice.a: Other details can still identify people (1), especially in small groups, e.g. "only Year 9 pupil in 9C" (1).

practice.q: Describe three things a good data story should include.
practice.a: Any three: clear question (1); headline finding (1); suitable labelled chart (1); context/limitations (1); recommendation/next step (1).
